chapter.sub: The river crests. The station is the only thing the valley can hear — and its building is in the flood zone.

items.text: SEASON 4 · EPISODE 10 · DRAFT · SEASON FINALE  Countdown · everyone · Level L4  The Kestrel River crests tonight. The station is the only thing the whole valley can hear. Its building is in the flood zone. Nobody is staying where the water goes.  ⚑ RV-97: emergency boundaries. RV-84: a flood, with no injury depicted. RV-98: figures illustrative. Most choices run on a clock.

items.title: Crest
items.stakes: The river crests tonight, higher than anyone here remembers. Thousands of people in the valley. Phones congested. The station is the only thing they can all hear — and its building is in the flood zone.
items.reward: Every word, to everyone, from a backup nobody has to stay behind to protect. And warning #14.

objectives.text: Obey the order and hand off
Route the second-language feed at the backup
Look closer: three things the river night keeps

items.rumor: An envelope in Maya's jacket says *open after the flood*. Tonight is the flood.

items.alt: The Old Mill gauge by the river at dusk in rain, the water high and fast, a barrier across the road in the foreground. A red marker near the top of the gauge reads 1964. Nobody is near the water.
items.caption: The Old Mill gauge, 6:40 p.m. The 1964 line is painted near the top.

lines.text: (The 1964 line is painted at the top of the gauge. Tonight the painted line is the forecast.)

items.alt: The newsroom in full emergency coverage. Vera holds a binder labelled FIELD SAFETY PLAN.

bubbles.text: Crew two stays at the high school shelter. Nobody on the river road after dark. That's the plan, and I own the plan.
And the agencies own the forecasts. We read them, word for word.

items.title: Page 1, handwritten margin
items.body: *1964: two reporters at the Old Mill bridge 'for the shot.' Both fine. Luck.* Vera's predecessor wrote it. Vera underlined *luck* in 2011, and again tonight.

items.alt: In master control, the official river forecast from the county and river agency on screen: crest at Old Mill expected between 11:30 p.m. and 12:30 a.m., near or above the 1964 level. Tess reads it.
items.caption: The forecast is theirs. The job is to get it to everyone, exactly.

items.prompt: (on headset) Maya, if we have to leave the building… who runs the valley?

options.label: “You do. From the backup. You've done it once at 2 a.m. Tonight's the same switcher.”
“Cal will.”
“Don't think about that yet.”
options.reply: I'm going to think about nothing else now.

items.prompt: 9:31. The agency's forecast just arrived. Omar is live. How does it go to air?
items.risk: Thousands of people deciding whether to leave.
timeout: Omar, unsure, ad-libs a version of it.
In a crisis, the exact words have to be decided before anyone speaks.

hints.text: Whose words are these, and who can't catch a paraphrase?

options.label: Omar summarizes it in his own words: “around midnight, give or take”
options.result: Some viewers hear 'midnight'; some hear 'give or take'. A shelter volunteer writes down 12:30.
options.consequence: A paraphrase changed the meaning for the people most at risk.
options.fail: In an emergency, the exact words and the source are the information.

options.label: Omar reads it word for word, names the agency, June captions it, and it repeats every fifteen minutes
options.result: The same words, every quarter hour, captioned, in both languages.
options.consequence: Nobody has to catch it the first time.

options.label: Engineering builds the station's own crest-time graphic from the gauge
options.result: Lena: “Is that the agency's number?” It isn't.
options.consequence: You're now a forecaster. You aren't one.
options.fail: Forecasts belong to the agencies. The station relays.

options.label: Hold it until a second source confirms
options.result: Twenty minutes pass. The agency is the source.
options.consequence: Delay on the one thing people need now.
options.fail: The official forecast is the confirmation.

items.alt: A newsroom phone line: a caller, shouting over rain, and Vera listening.

bubbles.text: The Old Mill bridge is open! I just drove it! Tell people!

items.prompt: 10:20. A caller insists the Old Mill bridge is open. Vera looks at you.
items.risk: Drivers heading for a closed bridge.
timeout: The report gets repeated on the newsroom floor until a producer nearly puts it in the crawl.

hints.text: Who knows whether the bridge is open?

options.label: Air it: “A viewer tells us the Old Mill bridge is open”
options.result: The EM's office calls within two minutes: closed since 10:15.
options.consequence: Thousands of drivers heard 'open' from the station they trust most tonight.
options.fail: An unverified report on the one channel everyone trusts is a hazard.

options.label: Route it to the emergency manager's desk and air only what's confirmed
options.result: EM: “Closed since 10:15. Thank you for not airing it.”
options.consequence: The valley hears the truth; the caller is thanked, not ignored.

options.label: Ignore the call
options.result: The caller calls back, angrier. So do three others.
options.consequence: Reports carry information; ignoring them loses it.

options.label: Send crew two to check the bridge
options.result: Vera: “Crew two stays at the shelter. That's the plan.”
options.consequence: You'd send people toward the river to check a rumor.
options.fail: Field crews move under Vera's safety plan, and not toward the water.

items.alt: Outside the main building in rain: Hank, the power vendor's technician in hi-vis, by a trailer generator with the facilities electrician's tape line between him and Maya.

bubbles.text: Utility's cut to the building. Your generator?
Mine and the electrician's. Transfer in ten seconds. Nobody touches the panel. Stay behind the tape.

items.caption: 11:10 p.m. The lights dip once. Then the generator carries the building.

lines.text: Didn't think I'd see you again after the festival.
You're on the other side of the tape. I'm on this side.
Best sentence I've heard from AV in two years. Stay there.

items.alt: Master control. Maya on the phone, very still.

bubbles.text: Water's in the lower lot. I'm ordering the main building evacuated. Everyone. Now.

items.caption: 11:40 p.m.

items.prompt: 11:40. The evacuation order includes you. The valley is watching the late coverage from this building.
items.risk: Your crew — and the valley's only channel.
timeout: People hesitate, looking at each other. A deputy walks in and repeats the order, less politely.

hints.text: Why did you drill the backup at 2 a.m.?

options.label: Stay twenty more minutes to finish the 11:00 update
options.result: The EM: “The order includes the station.” Rescuers now have to plan around you.
options.consequence: You made yourselves part of the emergency.
options.fail: Evacuation orders apply to the station too. The backup exists so nobody has to stay.

options.label: Hand master control to the backup by the runbook and leave — everyone
options.result: 11:42: the backup answers the handoff instantly. Tess, Maya and Omar take the high road across the valley.
options.consequence: The drill pays off: the valley stays on air and the building empties.

options.label: Leave without handing off
options.result: The valley's channel goes to slate as the crest arrives.
options.consequence: You obeyed the order and abandoned the valley.
options.fail: The handoff takes ninety seconds. It's in the runbook.

options.label: Everyone leaves except you
options.result: The EM sends a deputy back for you.
options.consequence: One person staying is still someone rescuers have to reach.

items.alt: The backup MCR across the valley. Cal at the desk, headset on, finger on the switcher, calm.

bubbles.text: Backup has the valley. Runbook page 3, named account. Go. Drive safe.

items.caption: 11:42 p.m.

items.title: 21:02 · Cal
items.body: One line, three hours before the order. In the 'reason' column: *#12.* Nothing else. He didn't tell anyone he was going. He just went where his own warning said nobody had ever been on a real night.

items.title: Cal was already there.
items.body: Nobody sent him. At 9 p.m., three hours before the order, Cal drove to the backup MCR and signed in with one word in the reason column: #12 — the backup has never run a real night. He read his own warning, and went to be where it said nobody had ever been.
items.label: Test: what made the handover safe?

items.alt: System View at 11:50 p.m.: the main MCR evacuated; the backup MCR on air through the IP link on the other carrier to Felix's transmitter and to the stream with captions; the second-language channel at the backup is not routed.
items.caption: Every output, from across the valley — almost.

items.alt: Tess arrives at the backup, soaked, and checks the outputs. Cal beside her.

bubbles.text: Second-language channel is carrying Omar. The interpreter isn't going anywhere.
The drill ran at 2 a.m. That feed's off air at 2 a.m.

lines.text: (typing at 180 words a minute) Every word. Every repeat. Every name of every agency.
(text) I'm reading every one, June. I'm at the shelter. It's warm.

items.title: The feed the drill couldn't see.
items.body: The second-language channel only runs during evening coverage, so the 2 a.m. drill never saw it. At the backup it's patched from the main audio. It's found at 11:52 — and fixed in minutes, because Ray's typed runbook, page 17, says exactly where the interpreter's feed lands at the backup.
items.label: Test: why didn't the drill catch it?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Tess beside a board. Time equals d over v: the agency's distance to the crest over its speed. Internal planning only — on air, the agency's words. Kilometres over kilometres an hour gives hours. Then tell me when we move master control.

bubbles.text: Time equals d over v: the agency's distance to the crest over its speed. Internal planning only — on air, the agency's words.
Kilometres over kilometres an hour gives hours.
Then tell me when we move master control.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Official alert   Evacuation order   Second-language channel   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Travel time  t = d ÷ v   t  time  d  distance  v  speed — keep units consistent (km and km/h give hours)

items.label: **Fix it:** route the second-language feed at the backup — Tess's hands.
**Learn it now:** emergency information — relay, verify, make it accessible.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · tap a plate to open it full size     What the room is telling you     Point it at people, not at the ceiling     Sound that brings people in

items.alt: A makeshift set at the backup: Omar mid-interview with a shelter coordinator. A red alert banner starts across the top: official alert, county emergency management.
items.caption: 12:20 a.m. An official alert arrives in the middle of a live interview.

items.prompt: 12:20. An official alert arrives during Omar's live interview with the shelter coordinator.
unknown: What the alert changes for viewers
items.risk: People who need the alert now.
timeout: The director hesitates; the alert sits in the queue for ninety seconds.
Alerts need a rule decided before the night: they go first.

hints.text: Which one belongs to the agency?

options.label: Let the interview finish — it's about shelters, it's relevant
options.result: Four minutes later the alert airs.
options.consequence: Four minutes is a long time in a flood.

options.label: The alert pre-empts: Omar stops, reads it word for word, captioned, both languages; the interview resumes after
options.result: The coordinator nods and waits. She wanted it to go first too.
options.consequence: The alert reaches everyone first and exactly.

options.label: Put it in the crawl only
options.result: People listening on radio and those who can't read quickly miss it.
options.consequence: A crawl isn't everyone.

options.label: Have Omar paraphrase it quickly to save time
options.result: He gets the street names in the wrong order.
options.consequence: Exact words are the information.

items.title: A system for the worst day
items.body: In 1963 the United States replaced its 1950s civil-defense radio plan with the Emergency Broadcast System, which let officials send warnings through ordinary radio and television stations. For decades it was known mostly for its test tone. Its real use came in floods, storms and fires, when local stations relayed official warnings to people who had no other way to hear them. The principle outlived the system: the station carries the official's words, exactly, to everyone.

items.alt: Vera, by phone from the shelter, on the line with field crew two.

bubbles.text: No. Not the bridge. Not for the crest shot. The plan says pull back, and I'm the plan.

items.caption: 12:40 a.m.

lines.text: Program solid on the IP link. Rain's biblical. Beacon's fine. I'm inside. I'm always inside.

items.prompt: 12:40. Crew two wants one live shot at the Old Mill bridge as the crest arrives. Vera has said no. The crew asks you to back them.
timeout: The crew waits in the car by the barrier, arguing. Vera orders them back again.
Every minute near the water is a minute of luck.

hints.text: Whose call is it — and is there a shot that doesn't need them there?

options.label: Back Vera: the plan says pull back; use the gauge camera the agency shares
options.result: The agency's gauge camera shows the crest. Crew two stays dry at the shelter.
options.consequence: The shot without the risk.

options.label: Suggest one shot from the car, engine running
options.result: Vera: “No.” The crew goes anyway. They're fine. It was luck.
options.consequence: You helped undermine the plan.
options.fail: Luck isn't a safety plan — the 1964 margin note says so.

options.label: Tell them it's their call
options.result: It isn't. It's Vera's.
options.consequence: You gave away someone else's authority.
options.fail: Field pull-backs belong to the field safety plan.

options.label: Stay out of it
options.result: The crew keeps arguing with Vera for ten minutes.
options.consequence: Silence prolongs the argument.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #41 · AVERY'S LENS  In a crisis, say less, more often  Emergency information should be short, repeated, sourced and accessible — the same words every time, captioned, with who said them.  Omar read the agency's words, named the agency, and repeated them every fifteen minutes. June captioned every one. Nobody paraphrased.

items.alt: The agency's gauge camera view: the river at its highest, just under the painted 1964 marker. A label: crest 1:10, minus 0.4 meters. The road and barrier are empty.
items.caption: 1:10 a.m. The crest passes forty centimeters under the 1964 line. Nobody is on the road.

items.alt: The backup MCR. Tess on the switcher, calm now, calling the next repeat of the forecast.

bubbles.text: Ready for the one-fifteen repeat. Captions, both languages. Take.

items.caption: Tess — not Maya — ran master control through the crest.

items.alt: Maya on the phone at the backup MCR.

bubbles.text: Three shelters. TV and radio. Captions, both languages. You're the only thing they can all hear. Thank you.

items.caption: Proof where the people are.

items.label: **Triage:** the last hour before the crest.

items.alt: Tess at the backup desk at 11:38 p.m. in red alarm light, headset on. Around her, stamped over the scene: generator ten minutes, STL falling, evacuate, captions?
narration: Everything above happened in order, one card at a time. At the desk it didn't. From 11:38 to 12:25 every failure touched every other one.
items.caption: Take Tess's chair. Keep the valley on air.

items.label: **☢ Meltdown:** the forty-seven minutes, all at once — contain, fail over, prove. Some systems on the map aren't yours.

items.alt: Dawn, clear and cold, at the backup site's lot with the ridge behind. Lena reads an email on her phone aloud to Maya.

bubbles.text: From the board: 'Thank you for last night. Master control moves to the regional hub in the spring.'

items.alt: Cal's fourteenth warning, handwritten on a card: fourteen. The hub has one clock, one building, and nobody who knows this valley. Signed C.
items.caption: Open it after the flood.

items.title: Warning #14
items.body: *The hub has one clock, one building, and nobody who knows this valley.* Folded inside: Cal's diagram of the hub, every arrow pointing to one room, 400 km away. And a smaller note: *If they build it anyway, make them drill it on a night like the one you just had. — C.*

items.alt: Cal's warnings on the wall, thirteen crossed out. Number fourteen, once missing, is now pinned beneath them: the hub.
items.caption: Thirteen crossed off. One that can't be crossed off by an engineer.

items.alt: Morning light. Maya alone in the lot, phone buzzing, answering.

bubbles.text: The hub vendor asked for you by name.

items.caption: END OF SEASON 4 · When the signal leaves the building, can the people at the other end trust what arrives? The boss level is next.

items.label: **Season 4 final:** twelve questions across On Air.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  On the worst night, relay the agencies' words exactly, repeat them, caption them, and carry every language. Route rumors to officials. Keep your hands off power that isn't yours. Obey the order — the backup exists so nobody has to stay — and check every output where the people are.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Tess ran the valley through the crest; Cal went where his own warning pointed. Who in your team would run the worst night if you weren't there — and have they rehearsed it?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't replace an evacuation plan.
